Theorem (Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions):
Given two coprime integers \(h\) and \(n\), there are infinitely many prime numbers \(p\) such that \(p\) is congruent to \(h\) modulo \(n\).

theorem Dirichlet:
  assumes "coprime h n"
  shows   "infinite {p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)}"
proof
  assume "finite {p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)}"
  then obtain K where K: "{p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)} ⊆ {..<K}"
    by (auto simp: finite_nat_iff_bounded)
  have "eventually (λx. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n) ∧ real p ≤ x. ln p / p) =
                        (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n). ln p / p)) at_top"
    using eventually_ge_at_top[of "real K"] by eventually_elim (intro sum.cong, use K in auto)
  hence "(λx. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n) ∧ real p ≤ x. ln p / p)) ∈ 
            Θ(λ_. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n). ln p / p))" by (intro bigthetaI_cong) auto
  also have "(λ_. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n). ln p / p)) ∈ O(λ_. 1)" by simp
  finally have "(λx. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n) ∧ real p ≤ x. ln p / p)) ∈ O(λ_. 1)" .
  from sum_in_bigo(2)[OF this Dirichlet_strong[OF assms]] and n show False by simp
qed

Theorem (Prime Implies Coprime):
If a number \(p\) is prime, then it is coprime with any other natural number \(n\) (i.e., \(p\) and \(n\) share no common divisors other than 1).

lemma prime_imp_coprime_nat [backward2]: "prime p ⟹ ¬ p dvd n ⟹ coprime p n" by auto2

Theorem (Prime Implies Coprime):
Given a prime number \(p\) and a number \(n\) that is not divisible by \(p\) (denoted as \(n \nmid p\)), it follows that \(p\) and \(n\) are coprime, meaning they share no common factors other than 1.

lemma prime_imp_coprime:
  assumes "prime p" "¬p dvd n"
  shows   "coprime p n"
  using assms by (simp add: prime_elem_imp_coprime)

This theorem asserts the existence of an integer \(k\) for a given pair of coprime numbers \(e\) and \(d\), where \(e\) is congruent to 1 modulo \(P-1\), and \(P\) and \(Q\) are distinct primes. The product \(e \cdot d\) can be expressed as one more than a multiple of \(P-1\).

lemma ex_k_mod:
  assumes coprime: "coprime (e :: nat) ((P-1)*(Q-1))" 
    and "P ≠ Q"
    and "prime P"
    and "prime Q"
    and "d ≠ 0"
    and " [e*d = 1] (mod (P-1))"
  shows "∃ k. e*d = 1 + k*(P-1)"
proof-
  have "e > 0"  
    using assms(1) assms(2) prime_gt_0_nat by fastforce
  then have "e*d ≥ 1" using assms by simp
  then obtain k where k: "e*d = 1 + k*(P-1)" 
    using assms(6) cong_to_1'_nat by auto
  then show ?thesis
    by simp
qed

Theorem (Distribution of Primes in Dirichlet Product):
Given a completely multiplicative function \(f\), the Dirichlet product of \(f\) with itself at a natural number \(n\) is equal to \(f(n)\) multiplied by the count of divisors of \(n\), expressed as \(\text{dirichlet_prod}(f, f)(n) = f(n) \times \text{divisor_count}(n)\).

lemma (in completely_multiplicative_function) dirichlet_prod_self:
  "dirichlet_prod f f n = f n * of_nat (divisor_count n)"
proof (cases "n = 0")
  case False
  have "dirichlet_prod f f n = (∑(r, d) | r * d = n. f (r * d))"
    by (simp add: dirichlet_prod_altdef2 mult)
  also have "… = (∑(r, d) | r * d = n. f n)"
    by (intro sum.cong) auto
  also have "… = f n * of_nat (card {(r, d). r * d = n})"
    by (simp add: mult.commute)
  also have "bij_betw fst {(r, d). r * d = n} {r. r dvd n}"
    by (rule bij_betwI[of _ _ _ "λr. (r, n div r)"]) (use False in auto)
  hence "card {(r, d). r * d = n} = card {r. r dvd n}"
    by (rule bij_betw_same_card)
  also have "… = divisor_count n"
    by (simp add: divisor_count_def)
  finally show ?thesis .
qed auto

Theorem (Prime Infinitude in Furstenberg Topology):
In the Furstenberg topology, where integers are viewed as residue classes, the set of prime numbers is infinite. This is shown by demonstrating that for any integer \(a\), the arithmetic progression \(a, a+b, a+2b, \ldots\) contains infinitely many distinct prime numbers.

lemma in_arith_progI [intro]: "[x = a] (mod b) ⟹ x ∈ arith_prog a b"
  by (auto simp: arith_prog_def)

Theorem (Modular Congruence for Distinct Primes):
Given two distinct prime numbers \(p\) and \(q\), and an integer \(a\) such that \(a\) is congruent to \(b\) modulo both \(p\) and \(q\) (i.e., \(a \mod p = b \mod p\) and \(a \mod q = b \mod q\)), and \(b\) is less than the product of \(p\) and \(q\) (\(b < p \cdot q\)), then \(a\) is also congruent to \(b\) modulo the product of \(p\) and \(q\) (i.e., \(a \mod (p \cdot q) = b\)).

lemma specializedtoprimes1a:
  fixes p::nat 
  shows "⟦prime p; prime q; p ≠ q; a mod p = b mod p; a mod q = b mod q; b < p*q ⟧
    ⟹ a mod (p*q) = b"
  by (simp add: specializedtoprimes1)

Theorem (Arithmetic Progression of Relatively Prime Integers):
Given a natural number \( n > 1 \), there exists a non-zero integer \( m \) and integers \( a \) and \( b \) such that the set of integers less than \( n \) that are relatively prime to \( n \) forms an arithmetic progression with common difference \( b \). This can be expressed as \( \{a + jb | j \in \mathbb{N} \text{ and } j < m\} \).

theorem arith_prog_rel_primes_solution:
  fixes n :: nat
  assumes ‹n > 1›
  shows ‹(prime n ∨ (∃ k. n = 2^k) ∨ n = 6) ⟷  
(∃ a b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {a+j*b| j::nat. j < m})›
proof-
  have ‹ (prime n ∨ (∃ k. n = 2^k) ∨  n = 6) ⟷
 (∃ b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m})›
  proof
    show "∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}"
      if "prime n ∨ (∃k. n = 2 ^ k) ∨ n = 6"
    proof-
      have "∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}"
        if "prime n"
      proof-
        have ‹∃m.   m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j| j::nat. j < m}›
        proof-
          have ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} =  {x | x :: nat. x ≠ 0 ∧ x < n}› 
          proof
            show "{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} ⊆ {x |x. x ≠ 0 ∧ x < n}"
              using prime_nat_iff'' that by fastforce
            show "{x |x. x ≠ 0 ∧ x < n} ⊆ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}"
              using coprime_commute prime_nat_iff'' that 
              by fastforce              
          qed
          obtain m where ‹m+1 = n›
            using add.commute assms less_imp_add_positive by blast
          have ‹{1+j| j::nat. j < (m::nat)} =  {x | x :: nat. x ≠ 0 ∧ x < m+1}› 
            by (metis Suc_eq_plus1   ‹m + 1 = n› gr0_implies_Suc le_simps(3)   less_nat_zero_code   linorder_not_less nat.simps(3) nat_neq_iff  plus_1_eq_Suc )
          hence  ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j| j::nat. j < (m::nat)}›
            using ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} =  {x | x :: nat. x ≠ 0 ∧ x < n}›  ‹m+1 = n› 
            by auto
          from ‹n > 1› have ‹m ≠ 0› 
            using ‹m + 1 = n› by linarith
          have ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j| j::nat. j < m}› 
            using Suc_eq_plus1 ‹1 < n› ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j |j. j < m}› 
            by auto
          hence ‹(∃ m.  m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j| j::nat. j < m})›
            using ‹m ≠ 0› 
            by blast
          thus ?thesis by blast
        qed
        hence ‹∃m.  m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*1| j::nat. j < m}›
          by auto
        thus ?thesis
          by blast 
      qed
      moreover have "∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}"
        if "∃k. n = 2 ^ k"
      proof-
        obtain k where ‹n = 2 ^ k›
          using ‹∃k. n = 2 ^ k› by auto
        have ‹k ≠ 0› 
          by (metis ‹1 < n› ‹n = 2 ^ k› nat_less_le power.simps(1))
        obtain t where ‹Suc t = k› 
          by (metis ‹k ≠ 0› fib.cases)
        have ‹n = 2^(Suc t)› 
          by (simp add: ‹Suc t = k› ‹n = 2 ^ k›)
        have ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*2| j::nat. j < 2^t}›
        proof
          show "{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} ⊆ {1 + j * 2 |j. j < 2^t}"
          proof
            fix x
            assume ‹x ∈ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}›
            hence ‹x < n›
              by blast
            have ‹coprime x n›
              using ‹x ∈ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}›
              by blast
            hence ‹coprime x (2^(Suc k))›
              by (simp add: ‹k ≠ 0› ‹n = 2 ^ k›)              
            have ‹odd x›
              using ‹coprime x n› ‹k ≠ 0› ‹n = 2 ^ k› 
              by auto 
            then obtain j where ‹x = 1+j*2›
              by (metis add.commute add.left_commute left_add_twice mult_2_right oddE)
            have ‹x < 2^k›
              using ‹n = 2 ^ k› ‹x < n› ‹x = 1+j*2› 
              by linarith
            hence ‹1+j*2 < 2^k›
              using ‹x = 1+j*2›
              by blast
            hence ‹j < 2^t›
              using ‹Suc t = k› by auto              
            thus ‹x ∈ {1 + j * 2 |j. j < 2^t}›
              using ‹x = 1+j*2›
              by blast
          qed
          show "{1 + j * 2 |j. j < 2 ^ t} ⊆ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}"
          proof
            fix x::nat
            assume ‹x ∈ {1 + j * 2 |j. j < 2 ^ t}›
            then obtain j where ‹x = 1 + j * 2› and ‹j < 2 ^ t›
              by blast
            have ‹x < 2*(2^t)›
              using  ‹x = 1 + j * 2›  ‹j < 2 ^ t›
              by linarith              
            hence ‹x < n›
              by (simp add: ‹n = 2 ^ Suc t›)
            moreover have ‹coprime x n›
              by (metis (no_types) ‹⋀thesis. (⋀j. ⟦x = 1 + j * 2; j < 2 ^ t⟧ ⟹ thesis) ⟹ thesis› ‹n = 2 ^ k› coprime_Suc_left_nat coprime_mult_right_iff coprime_power_right_iff plus_1_eq_Suc)              
            ultimately show ‹x ∈ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}›
              by blast
          qed
        qed
        have ‹(2::nat)^(t::nat) ≠ 0› 
          by simp
        obtain m where ‹m = (2::nat)^t› by blast
        have ‹m ≠ 0› 
          using ‹m = 2 ^ t› 
          by auto
        have ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*2| j::nat. j < m}›
          using ‹m = 2 ^ t› ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * 2 |j. j < 2 ^ t}› 
          by auto
        from  ‹m ≠ 0›  ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*2| j::nat. j < m}›
        show ?thesis by blast
      qed
      moreover have "∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}"
        if "n = 6"
      proof-
        have  ‹{x | x. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6} = {1+j*4| j::nat. j < 2}›
        proof-
          have ‹{x | x::nat. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6} = {1, 5}›
          proof
            show "{u. ∃x. u = (x::nat) ∧ x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6} ⊆ {1, 5}"
            proof
              fix u::nat
              assume ‹u ∈ {u. ∃x. u = x ∧ x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6}›
              hence ‹coprime u 6›
                by blast
              have ‹u < 6›
                using ‹u ∈ {u. ∃x. u = x ∧ x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6}›
                by blast
              moreover have ‹u ≠ 0›
                using ‹coprime u 6› ord_eq_0 
                by fastforce
              moreover have ‹u ≠ 2›
                using ‹coprime u 6›
                by auto
              moreover have ‹u ≠ 3›
              proof-
                have ‹gcd (3::nat) 6 = 3›
                  by auto
                thus ?thesis 
                  by (metis (no_types) ‹coprime u 6› ‹gcd 3 6 = 3› coprime_iff_gcd_eq_1 
                      numeral_eq_one_iff semiring_norm(86))
              qed
              moreover have ‹u ≠ 4›
              proof-
                have ‹gcd (4::nat) 6 = 2›
                  by (metis (no_types, lifting) add_numeral_left gcd_add1 gcd_add2 gcd_nat.idem
                      numeral_Bit0 numeral_One one_plus_numeral semiring_norm(4) semiring_norm(5))
                thus ?thesis
                  using ‹coprime u 6› coprime_iff_gcd_eq_1 
                  by auto 
              qed
              ultimately have ‹u = 1 ∨ u = 5›
                by auto
              thus ‹u ∈ {1, 5}›
                by blast
            qed
            show "{1::nat, 5} ⊆ {x |x. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6}"
            proof-
              have ‹(1::nat) ∈ {x |x. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6}›
                by simp                
              moreover have ‹(5::nat) ∈ {x |x. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6}›
                by (metis Suc_numeral coprime_Suc_right_nat less_add_one mem_Collect_eq
                    numeral_plus_one semiring_norm(5) semiring_norm(8))                
              ultimately show ?thesis 
                by blast
            qed
          qed
          moreover have ‹{1+j*4| j::nat. j < 2} = {1, 5}›
            by auto
          ultimately show ?thesis by auto
        qed
        moreover have ‹(2::nat) ≠ 0›
          by simp          
        ultimately have ‹∃ m.  m ≠ 0 ∧ {x | x :: nat. x < 6 ∧ coprime x 6} = {1+j*4| j::nat. j < m}›
          by blast
        thus ?thesis
          using that 
          by auto 
      qed
      ultimately show ?thesis
        using that 
        by blast 
    qed
    show "prime n ∨ (∃k. n = 2 ^ k) ∨ n = 6"
      if "∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}"
    proof-
      obtain b m where ‹m ≠ 0› and ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}›
        using ‹∃b m. m ≠ 0 ∧ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
        by auto
      show ?thesis
      proof(cases ‹n = 2›)
        case True
        thus ?thesis
          by auto 
      next
        case False
        have ‹b ≤ 4›
        proof(cases ‹odd b›)
          case True
          show ?thesis
          proof(rule classical)
            assume ‹¬(b ≤ 4)›
            hence ‹b > 4› 
              using le_less_linear 
              by blast
            obtain m where ‹m ≠ 0› 
              and ‹{x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}›
              using ‹m ≠ 0› ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
              by blast
            have ‹b ≠ 0› 
              using ‹4 < b› 
              by linarith
            have ‹n = 2 + (m-1)*b› 
            proof-
              have ‹n-1 ∈ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                using ‹1 < n› coprime_diff_one_left_nat 
                by auto
              have ‹n-1 ∈ {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}› 
                using ‹n - 1 ∈ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                  ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
                by blast
              then obtain i::nat where ‹n-1 = 1+i*b› and ‹i < m› 
                by blast
              have ‹i ≤ m-1› 
                using ‹i < m› 
                by linarith
              have ‹1 + (m-1)*b ∈ {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}› 
                using ‹m ≠ 0› 
                by auto
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ∈ {x | x::nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                using ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
                by blast
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b < n› 
                by blast
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ≤ n-1› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ≤ 1+i*b› 
                using ‹n - 1 = 1 + i * b› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹(m-1)*b ≤ i*b› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹m-1 ≤ i› 
                using ‹b ≠ 0› 
                by auto
              hence ‹m-1 = i› 
                using ‹i ≤ m - 1› le_antisym 
                by blast
              thus ?thesis 
                using ‹m ≠ 0› ‹n - 1 = 1 + i * b› 
                by auto
            qed
            have ‹m ≥ 2› 
              using ‹n = 2 + (m - 1)*b› ‹n ≠ 2› 
              by auto
            hence ‹1+b ∈ {1+j*b| j. j < m}› 
              by fastforce
            hence  ‹1+b ∈ {x | x::nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}›
              using ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
              by blast
            hence ‹coprime (1+b) n› 
              by blast
            have ‹(2::nat) dvd (1+b)› 
              using ‹odd b› 
              by simp
            hence ‹coprime (2::nat) n› 
              using ‹coprime (1 + b) n› coprime_common_divisor coprime_left_2_iff_odd odd_one 
              by blast
            have ‹(2::nat) < n› 
              using ‹1 < n› ‹n ≠ 2› 
              by linarith
            have ‹2 ∈ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
              using ‹2 < n› ‹coprime 2 n› 
              by blast 
            hence  ‹2 ∈ {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}› 
              using ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
              by blast
            then obtain j::nat where ‹2 = 1+j*b› 
              by blast 
            have  ‹1 = j*b› 
              using ‹2 = 1+j*b›
              by linarith
            thus ?thesis 
              by simp
          qed
        next
          case False
          hence ‹even b›
            by simp
          show ?thesis
          proof(rule classical)
            assume ‹¬(b ≤ 4)›
            hence ‹b > 4› 
              using le_less_linear 
              by blast
            obtain m where  ‹ m ≠ 0›
              and ‹{x | x::nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}›
              using ‹m ≠ 0› ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
              by blast
            have ‹b ≠ 0› 
              using ‹4 < b› 
              by linarith
            have ‹n = 2 + (m-1)*b› 
            proof-
              have ‹n-1 ∈ {x | x::nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                using ‹1 < n› coprime_diff_one_left_nat 
                by auto
              have ‹n-1 ∈ {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}› 
                using ‹n - 1 ∈ {x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                  ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
                by blast
              then obtain i::nat where ‹n-1 = 1+i*b› and ‹i < m› 
                by blast
              have ‹i ≤ m-1› 
                using ‹i < m› 
                by linarith
              have ‹1 + (m-1)*b ∈ {1+j*b| j::nat. j < m}› 
                using ‹m ≠ 0› 
                by auto
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ∈ {x | x :: nat. x < n ∧ coprime x n}› 
                using ‹{x |x. x < n ∧ coprime x n} = {1 + j * b |j. j < m}› 
                by blast
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b < n› 
                by blast
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ≤ n-1› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹1 + (m-1)*b ≤ 1+i*b› 
                using ‹n - 1 = 1 + i * b› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹(m-1)*b ≤ i*b› 
                by linarith
              hence ‹m-1 ≤ i› 
                using ‹b ≠ 0› 
                by auto
              hence ‹m-1 = i› 
                using ‹i ≤ m - 1› le_antisym 
                by blast
              thus ?thesis 
                using ‹m ≠ 0› ‹n - 1 = 1 + i * b› 
                by auto
            qed
            obtain k :: nat where ‹b = 2*k› 
              using ‹even b›
              by blast
            have ‹n = 2*(1 + (m-1)*k)›
              using  ‹n = 2 + (m-1)*b›  ‹b = 2*k› 
              by simp
            show ?thesis
            proof (cases ‹odd m›)
              case True
              hence ‹odd m› by blast
              then obtain t::nat where ‹m-1 = 2*t› 
                by (metis odd_two_times_div_two_nat)
              have  ‹n = 2*(1 + b*t)› 
                using ‹m - 1 = 2 * t› ‹n = 2 + (m - 1) * b›

Theorem (Probabilistic Primality Testing):
This theorem addresses the concept of probabilistic primality tests, which are algorithms that determine with high probability whether a given number is prime or composite. Specifically, it states that for a given integer \(p\), if \(p\) is prime, then for any integer \(a\), \(a\) is not coprime to \(p\) (i.e., \(a\) shares a common factor with \(p\)), which is a condition used in tests like Miller-Rabin, Solovay-Strassen, and Fermat. The theorem uses congruence relations to express this relationship, where \(a \equiv 0 \mod p\) if and only if \(a\) and \(p\) are not coprime.

lemma prime_cong_eq_0_iff: "prime p ⟹ [a = 0] (mod p) ⟷ ¬coprime a p" for a p :: int
  using not_coprime_cong_eq_0[of p a] cong_eq_0_not_coprime[of p a]
  by auto

Theorem (Solving Coprime Diophantine Equations):
Given two coprime natural numbers \(a\) and \(n\), there exists a natural number \(x\) such that \(a \cdot x \equiv 1 \mod n\). This theorem is a formalization of the fact that for any two coprime numbers, there is a multiplicative inverse modulo \(n\), which is crucial in solving certain types of Diophantine equations.

Theorem (Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions):
Given two coprime integers \(h\) and \(n\), there are infinitely many prime numbers \(p\) such that \(p\) is congruent to \(h\) modulo \(n\).

theorem Dirichlet:
  assumes "coprime h n"
  shows   "infinite {p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)}"
proof
  assume "finite {p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)}"
  then obtain K where K: "{p. prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n)} ⊆ {..<K}"
    by (auto simp: finite_nat_iff_bounded)
  have "eventually (λx. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n) ∧ real p ≤ x. ln p / p) =
                        (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n). ln p / p)) at_top"
    using eventually_ge_at_top[of "real K"] by eventually_elim (intro sum.cong, use K in auto)
  hence "(λx. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n) ∧ real p ≤ x. ln p / p)) ∈

  also have "(λ_. (∑p | prime p ∧ [p = h] (mod n). ln p / p)) ∈ O(λ_. 1)" by simp

  from sum_in_bigo(2)[OF this Dirichlet_strong[OF assms]] and n show False by simp
qed

Theorem (Arithmetic Progression of Relatively Prime Integers):
Given a natural number \( n > 1 \), there exists a non-zero integer \( m \) and integers \( a \) and \( b \) such that the set of integers less than \( n \) that are relatively prime to \( n \) forms an arithmetic progression with common difference \( b \). Theorem (Prime Numbers Coprime):
If \(p\) and \(q\) are prime numbers, then they are coprime, meaning they have no common factors other than 1.

lemma primes_coprime:
  "prime p ⟹ prime q ⟹ p ≠ q ⟹ coprime p q"
  using prime_imp_coprime primes_dvd_imp_eq by blast

Theorem (Equivalence of Units and Totatives):
In a given number system, the set of units (elements that have a multiplicative inverse) is equivalent to the set of totatives (positive integers less than the number that are coprime to it). This is fundamental in probabilistic primality testing, where randomness and coprimality play key roles in distinguishing prime numbers from composites.

lemma Units_eq: "Units R = totatives n"
proof safe
  fix x assume x: "x ∈ Units R"
  then obtain y where y: "[x * y = 1] (mod n)"
    using n_gt_1 by (auto simp: Units_def cong_def)
  hence "coprime x n"
    using cong_imp_coprime cong_sym coprime_1_left coprime_mult_left_iff by metis
  with x show "x ∈ totatives n" by (auto simp: totatives_def Units_def intro!: Nat.gr0I)
next
  fix x assume x: "x ∈ totatives n"
  then obtain y where "y < n" "[x * y = 1] (mod n)"
    using coprime_iff_invertible'_nat[of n x] by (auto simp: totatives_def)
  with x show "x ∈ Units R"
    using n_gt_1 by (auto simp: Units_def mult_ac cong_def totatives_less)
qed

Theorem (Coprimality of Integer and Natural Number Representations):
Given an integer \(p\) and its representation in a ring structure, the integer \(p\) and its natural number counterpart are coprime if and only if \(p\) itself is coprime to its natural number representation.

lemma coprime_nat_int: "coprime (int p) (to_int_mod_ring pr) ⟷ coprime p (nat(to_int_mod_ring pr))"

Theorem (Coprimality of Natural Numbers and Gaussian Integers):
Given two natural numbers \(a\) and \(b\), if they are coprime in the context of Gaussian integers (denoted as \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}[i]\)), then their coprimality in the set of natural numbers (\(\mathbb{N}\)) is equivalent to their greatest common divisor (gcd) being 1.

lemma coprime_of_nat_gauss_int: "coprime (of_nat a :: gauss_int) (of_nat b) = coprime a b"
  unfolding coprime_iff_gcd_eq_1 gcd_of_nat_gauss_int by auto

Theorem (Probabilistic Primality Testing):
Given a natural number \(a\), if \(p\) is a prime number, then \(a\) and \(p\) are coprime, meaning they share no common factors other than 1. This is expressed as \(a\) being coprime with \(p\) if and only if \(p\) does not divide \(a\) (denoted as \(p \nmid a\)). This relationship is crucial in probabilistic primality tests, which assess the likelihood of a number being prime based on the absence of common divisors with randomly chosen numbers.

lemma p_coprime_right_nat: "prime p ⟹ coprime a p = (¬ p dvd a)" for p a :: nat
  by (meson coprime_absorb_left coprime_commute not_prime_unit prime_imp_coprime_nat)

Theorem (Congruence of Product of Coprime Natural Numbers Modulo Product):
Given two natural numbers \(x\) and \(y\) that are congruent modulo the product of a set of pairwise coprime natural numbers \(A\), their product \(x \cdot y\) is congruent to their product modulo the product of the numbers in \(A\).

lemma cong_cong_prod_coprime_nat:
  "[x = y] (mod (∏i∈A. m i))" if
    "(∀i∈A. [x = y] (mod m i))"
    "(∀i∈A. (∀j∈A. i ≠ j ⟶ coprime (m i) (m j)))"
  for x y :: nat
  using that by (induct A rule: infinite_finite_induct)
    (auto intro!: coprime_cong_mult_nat prod_coprime_right)

Theorem (Cayley-Hamilton for a Matrix):
Given a square matrix \(C\), the Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that \(C\) satisfies its own characteristic equation, meaning \(C^n + a_{n-1}C^{n-1} + \ldots + a_1C + a_0I = 0\), where \(I\) is the identity matrix and \(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}\) are the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of \(C\).

lemma C_0[simp]: "C 0 = 0"
  by (simp add: C_def)

The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix over a commutative ring satisfies its own characteristic equation. Formally, if \(A\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix with characteristic polynomial \(p(\lambda)\), then \(p(A) = 0\), where \(0\) is the zero matrix of the same size.

  fix A :: "'n ⇒ 'n ⇒ 'a" assume neq: "⋀i j. i ≠ j ⟹ A i j = 0"
  let ?pp = "λp. of_int (sign p) * (∏i∈UNIV. A i (p i))"

  { fix p :: "'n ⇒ 'n" assume p: "p permutes UNIV" "p ≠ id"
    then obtain i where i: "i ≠ p i"
      unfolding id_def by metis
    with neq[OF i] have "(∏i∈UNIV. A i (p i)) = 0"

  then have "(∑p | p permutes UNIV. ?pp p) = (∑p∈{id}. ?pp p)"
    by (intro sum.mono_neutral_cong_right) (auto intro: permutes_id)
  then show "(∑p | p permutes UNIV. ?pp p) = (∏i∈UNIV. A i i)"
     by (simp add: sign_id)
qed

  shows "(⋀i j. i ≠ j ⟹ to_fun A i j = 0) ⟹ det A = (∏i∈UNIV. to_fun A i i)"
proof transfer
  fix A :: "'n ⇒ 'n ⇒ 'a" assume neq: "⋀i j. i ≠ j ⟹ A i j = 0"
  let ?pp = "λp. of_int (sign p) * (∏i∈UNIV. A i (p i))"

  { fix p :: "'n ⇒ 'n" assume p: "p permutes UNIV" "p ≠ id"
    then obtain i where i: "i ≠ p i"
      unfolding id_def by metis
    with neq[OF i] have "(∏i∈UNIV. A i (p i)) = 0"
      by (intro prod_zero) auto }
  then have "(∑p | p permutes UNIV. ?pp p) = (∑p∈{id}. ?pp p)"
    by (intro sum.mono_neutral_cong_right) (auto intro: permutes_id)
  then show "(∑p | p permutes UNIV. ?pp p) = (∏i∈UNIV. A i i)"
     by (simp add: sign_id)
qed

  by (induction I rule: infinite_finite_induct)
     (simp_all add: smult_right_add vec_eq_iff)

For a prime number \(p\), the factorial of \(p-1\) is congruent to \(-1\) modulo \(p\), expressed as \((p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\).

lemma wilson_theorem:
  assumes "prime p"
  shows "[fact (p - 1) = - 1] (mod p)"
proof (cases "p = 2")
  case True
  then show ?thesis
    by (simp add: cong_def fact_prod)
next
  case False
  then show ?thesis
    using assms prime_ge_2_nat
    by (metis residues_prime.wilson_theorem1 residues_prime.intro le_eq_less_or_eq)
qed

Theorem (Wilson's Theorem for Prime Numbers):
Given a prime number \(p > 2\), it holds that \((p - 1)\) is congruent to \(-1\) modulo \(p\), expressed as \((p - 1) \equiv -1 \pmod{p}\).

lemma (in residues_prime) wilson_theorem1:
  assumes a: "p > 2"
  shows "[fact (p - 1) = (-1::int)] (mod p)"
proof -
  let ?Inverse_Pairs = "{{x, inv x}| x. x ∈ Units R - {𝟭, ⊖ 𝟭}}"
  have UR: "Units R = {𝟭, ⊖ 𝟭} ∪ ⋃?Inverse_Pairs"
    by auto
  have 11: "𝟭 ≠ ⊖ 𝟭"
    using a one_eq_neg_one by force
  have "(⨂i∈Units R. i) = (⨂i∈{𝟭, ⊖ 𝟭}. i) ⊗ (⨂i∈⋃?Inverse_Pairs. i)"
    apply (subst UR)
    apply (subst finprod_Un_disjoint)
    using inv_one inv_eq_neg_one_eq apply (auto intro!: funcsetI)+
    done
  also have "(⨂i∈{𝟭, ⊖ 𝟭}. i) = ⊖ 𝟭"
    by (simp add: 11)
  also have "(⨂i∈(⋃?Inverse_Pairs). i) = (⨂A∈?Inverse_Pairs. (⨂y∈A. y))"
    by (rule finprod_Union_disjoint) (auto simp: pairwise_def disjnt_def dest!: inv_eq_imp_eq)
  also have "… = 𝟭"
    apply (rule finprod_one_eqI)
    apply clarsimp
    apply (subst finprod_insert)
        apply auto
    apply (metis inv_eq_self)
    done
  finally have "(⨂i∈Units R. i) = ⊖ 𝟭"
    by simp
  also have "(⨂i∈Units R. i) = (⨂i∈Units R. i mod p)"
    by (rule finprod_cong') (auto simp: res_units_eq)
  also have "… = (∏i∈Units R. i) mod p"
    by (rule prod_cong) auto
  also have "… = fact (p - 1) mod p"
    using assms
    by (simp add: res_prime_units_eq int_prod zmod_int prod_int_eq fact_prod)
  finally have "fact (p - 1) mod p = ⊖ 𝟭" .
  then show ?thesis
    by (simp add: cong_def res_neg_eq res_one_eq zmod_int)
qed

Theorem (Probabilistic Primality Testing):
This theorem addresses the concept of probabilistic primality tests, which are algorithms that determine with high probability whether a given number is prime or composite. Specifically, it states that for a given integer \(p\), if \(p\) is prime, then for any integer \(a\), \(a\) is not coprime to \(p\) (i.e., \(a\) shares a common factor with \(p\)), which is a condition used in tests like Miller-Rabin, Solovay-Strassen, and Fermat. The theorem uses congruence relations to express this relationship, where \(a \equiv 0 \mod p\) if and only if \(a\) and \(p\) are not coprime.

lemma prime_cong_eq_0_iff: "prime p ⟹ [a = 0] (mod p) ⟷ ¬coprime a p" for a p :: int
  using not_coprime_cong_eq_0[of p a] cong_eq_0_not_coprime[of p a]
  by auto

Theorem (Primeness Condition in Factorial Monoid):
In a factorial monoid \(G\), the primeness condition states that an element \(g\) is prime if it is not a unit and whenever \(g\) divides a product \(ab\), it must divide at least one of \(a\) or \(b\).

lemma (in factorial_monoid) primeness_condition: "primeness_condition_monoid G" ..

Theorem (Existence of Prime Factorization for Natural Numbers):
For any positive natural number \(n\), there exists a set of prime numbers \(M\) such that \(n\) is equal to the product of all primes in \(M\).

  "n > 0 ⟹ (∃M. (∀p::nat ∈ set_mset M. prime p) ∧ n = (∏i ∈# M. i))"
  using prime_factorization_exists[of n] by auto

Theorem (Prime Integer Characterization):
Given an integer \(p \geq 2\), it is prime if and only if whenever \(p\) divides the product of any two integers \(m\) and \(n\), then \(p\) must divide at least one of those integers \(m\) or \(n\).

lemma prime_intI:
  "prime p" if "p ≥ 2" and "⋀m n. p dvd m * n ⟹ p dvd m ∨ p dvd n" for p :: int
  using that by (auto intro!: primeI prime_elemI)

Theorem (Prime Factors of a Factorial):
For any natural number \(n\), the set of prime factors of \(n!\) (factorial of \(n\)) is the set of all prime numbers less than or equal to \(n\).

lemma prime_factors_fact:
  "prime_factors (fact n) = {p ∈ {2..n}. prime p}" (is "?M = ?N")
proof (rule set_eqI)
  fix p
  { fix m :: nat
    assume "p ∈ prime_factors m"
    then have "prime p" and "p dvd m" by auto
    moreover assume "m > 0" 
    ultimately have "2 ≤ p" and "p ≤ m"
      by (auto intro: prime_ge_2_nat dest: dvd_imp_le)
    moreover assume "m ≤ n"
    ultimately have "2 ≤ p" and "p ≤ n"
      by (auto intro: order_trans)
  } note * = this
  show "p ∈ ?M ⟷ p ∈ ?N"
    by (auto simp add: fact_prod prime_factors_prod Suc_le_eq dest!: prime_prime_factors intro: *)
qed

Theorem (Existence of Prime Factors):
For any natural number \(n\) greater than 1, there exists at least one prime number \(p\) such that \(p\) is a factor of \(n\).

lemma prime_factors_elem:
  fixes n :: nat assumes "1 < n" shows "∃p. p ∈ prime_factors n"
  using assms by (cases "prime n") (auto simp: prime_factors_dvd prime_factor_nat)

Theorem (Uniqueness of Factorization into Primes):
For any two sets of prime numbers, if their products are equal, then the sets themselves must be identical. In other words, if the product of all primes in one set equals the product of all primes in another set, then those two sets of primes are the same.

theorem factorization_unique:
  "∀p∈#M. prime p ⟹ ∀p∈#N. prime p ⟹ (∏i∈#M. i) = (∏i∈#N. i) ⟹ M = N"
@proof @have "M ⊆# N" @qed

next
  case False
  then have "m < n" by simp
  then show ?thesis by (simp add: ffact_nat_triv)
qed

Theorem (Cardinality of Multiset Powerset):
Given a finite set A, the cardinality of the multiset powerset (the set of all multisets that can be formed from A) is less than or equal to one plus the cardinality of A.

lemma count_mset_set_leq':
  assumes "finite A"
  shows "count (mset_set A) x ≤ Suc 0"
using assms count_mset_set_leq by fastforce

Theorem (Subset Relation between a Set of Sets and the Original Set):
Given a set \(A\), the collection of all subsets of \(A\) forms a subset of \(A\) itself, denoted as \(mset(set_mset A) \subseteq A\).

lemma mset_set_set_mset_msubset: "mset_set (set_mset A) ⊆# A"
proof (rule mset_subset_eqI)
  fix x show "count (mset_set (set_mset A)) x ≤ count A x"
    by (cases "x ∈# A") simp_all
qed

Theorem (Count of Elements in a Subset):
If set A is a subset of set B, then the number of elements in A is less than or equal to the number of elements in B.

lemma mset_subset_eq_count:
  "A ⊆# B ⟹ count A a ≤ count B a"
  by (simp add: subseteq_mset_def)

Theorem (Power Set Enumeration Equivalence):
Given a set \(X\), the set of all subsets of \(X\) (its power set) can be enumerated by mapping each subset to a unique element in a powerset, ensuring no duplicates. Formally, this is expressed as \(\mathcal{P}(X) = \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\{X\})\), where \(\mathcal{P}\) denotes the powerset operation.

theorem powerset_enum_correct: "set (map set (powerset_enum xs)) = Pow (set xs)"
proof(standard)
  show "set (map set (powerset_enum xs)) ⊆ Pow (set xs)"
    using filter_bool_list_not_elem by fastforce
next
  have "⋀x. x ⊆ set xs ⟹ x ∈ (λx. set (filter_bool_list x xs)) ` {zs. length zs = length xs}"
    unfolding image_def using filter_bool_list_exist_length image_def by auto
  then show "Pow (set xs) ⊆ set (map set (powerset_enum xs))"
    using all_bool_lists_correct by auto
qed

Theorem (Subset Relationship between Numbers and Total Functions):
Given that "NUM" is a subset of "TOTAL" functions, and considering the properties of finite subsets and partial recursive functions, it is established that "NUM" is also a subset of "CP" (complementary partial recursive functions) and "TOTAL". This relationship is proven using automated reasoning.

theorem NUM_subset_TOTAL: "NUM ⊂ TOTAL"
  using CP_subseteq_TOTAL FIN_not_subseteq_NUM FIN_subseteq_CP NUM_subseteq_TOTAL
  by auto

Theorem (Total Subset Relation):
The set of all total functions is a subset of the class of computable functions. This is established by showing that any total function, which is defined for all inputs, can be computed, hence belonging to the class of computable functions.

theorem TOTAL_subset_CONS: "TOTAL ⊂ CONS"
  using TOTAL_subseteq_CONS TOTAL_neq_CONS by simp

If for every element in multiset A, the count of that element in A is less than or equal to the count of the same element in multiset B, then A is a subset of B, denoted as \(A \subseteq B\).

lemma mset_subset_eqI:
  "(⋀a. count A a ≤ count B a) ⟹ A ⊆# B"
  by (simp add: subseteq_mset_def)

If set A is a subset of set B, then the power set of A (the set of all subsets of A) is also a subset of the power set of B.

lemma fPowD: "A |∈| fPow B ⟹ A |⊆| B"
  by (rule PowD[Transfer.transferred])

Theorem (Cardinality of Powers of a Set):
Given a set \(A\), the cardinality of the power set \(Pow A\) (the set of all subsets of \(A\)) is strictly greater than the cardinality of \(A\) itself, as shown by Cantor's theorem.

  using card_of_ordLess2[of "Pow A" A]  Cantors_theorem[of A]
    Pow_not_empty[of A] by auto

lemma PowI: "A ⊆ B ⟹ A ∈ Pow B"
  by (simp add: Pow_def)

lemma card_lists_length_le:

    by (subst card_UN_disjoint)
       (auto simp add: card_lists_length_eq finite_lists_length_eq)
  also have "(⋃i≤n. {xs. set xs ⊆ A ∧ length xs = i}) = {xs. set xs ⊆ A ∧ length xs ≤ n}"
    by auto
  finally show ?thesis by simp
qed

Theorem (Cardinality of Finite Sets of k-Sets):
For a finite set \(N\) and a positive integer \(k\), the number of \(k\)-sets (subsets of size \(k\)) that can be formed from \(N\) is equal to the binomial coefficient \(\binom{N}{k}\), which represents the number of ways to choose \(k\) elements from \(N\).

lemma card_finsets: "finite N ⟹ card (finsets N k) = card N choose k"
  by (simp add: finsets_def n_subsets)

Theorem (Sum of Finite Sets):
Given a non-empty set \(S\), the set of all n-tuples formed from \(S\) is also finite.

lemma tuples_finite [simp]: ‹⟦ finite (S::'a set); S ≠ {} ⟧ ⟹ finite (tuples S n :: 'a list set)›
  by (auto simp add: tuples_def dest: finite_lists_length_eq)

Theorem (Existence of Cardinality for Finite Sets):
For any finite set \(S\), there exists a natural number \(n\) such that the cardinality (number of elements) of \(S\) is exactly \(n\).

lemma ex_card: "finite S ⟹ ∃ n:: nat. card S = n"
by simp

Theorem (Cardinality of Multiset Powerset):
Given a finite set A, the cardinality of the multiset powerset (the set of all multisets that can be formed from A) is less than or equal to one plus the cardinality of A.

lemma count_mset_set_leq':
  assumes "finite A"
  shows "count (mset_set A) x ≤ Suc 0"
using assms count_mset_set_leq by fastforce

Theorem (Correct Enumeration of Combinatorial Objects):
Given a set of distinct elements \(X\), the set obtained by mapping each element to its n-subsets, enumerated by \(n_subset_enum\), is equal to the set of all n-subsets of \(X\), denoted as \(n_subsets(X)\). Formally, \(\forall distinct xs, \text{set} \left(\text{map set} (\text{n\_subset\_enum} xs n)\right) = n\_subsets(set(xs)) n\).

theorem n_subset_enum_correct:
  "distinct xs ⟹ set (map set (n_subset_enum xs n)) = n_subsets (set xs) n"
proof(standard)
  show "distinct xs ⟹ set (map set (n_subset_enum xs n)) ⊆ n_subsets (set xs) n"
    using n_subset_enum_correct_aux1 n_bool_lists_correct by auto
next
  show "distinct xs ⟹ n_subsets (set xs) n ⊆ set (map set (n_subset_enum xs n))"
    using n_subset_enum_correct_aux2 by auto
qed

Theorem (Representation of a Number in a Finite Set):
If a set \(B\) is finite, then the number of elements \(x\) in \(B\) that are also in a given subset \(b\) is equal to the cardinality of \(B\), expressed as \(\text{rep}_x(B) = |B|\), where \(\text{rep}_x(B)\) counts the occurrences of \(x\) in the subsets of \(B\).

lemma rep_number_on_set_def: "finite B ⟹ (mset_set B) rep x = card {b ∈ B . x ∈ b}"
  by (simp add: point_replication_number_def)

Theorem (Existence of Cardinality for Finite Sets):
For any finite set \(S\), there exists a natural number \(n\) such that the cardinality (number of elements) of \(S\) is exactly \(n\).

lemma ex_card: "finite S ⟹ ∃ n:: nat. card S = n"
by simp

Theorem (Count of Subsets in Combinatorial Design):
Given a base set \( \mathcal{B} \) and a subset \( p \) of \( \mathcal{B} \) with exactly two elements, the count of specific subsets \( y \) within the intersection of \( p \) and a set \( b_2 \), excluding \( \mathcal{B} \), is one less than the total count of such subsets. Formally, if \( p \subseteq \mathcal{B} \) and \( |p| = 2 \), then \( \text{count} \left( \sum_{\substack{y \subseteq p \cap b_2 \\ |y| = 2}} b_2 \right) \in \mathcal{B} - \{p\} = \Lambda - 1 \).

lemma sym_sum_mset_inter2_sets_count: 
  assumes "blv ∈# ℬ"
  assumes "p ⊆ blv"
  assumes "card p = 2"
  shows "count (∑⇩#{#mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2}. b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#})#}) p = Λ - 1" 
    (is "count (∑⇩#?M) p = Λ - 1")
proof -
  have size_inter: "size {# mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2} | b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b2#} 
      = Λ - 1"
    using bibd_subset_occ assms by simp
  have "∀ b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b2 ⟶ count (mset_set{y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2}) p = 1"
    using assms(2) count_mset_set(1) assms(3) by (auto simp add: assms(1) finite_blocks)
  then have "∀ bl ∈# {#b1 ∈#(ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b1#}. 
      count (mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ bl ∧ card y = 2}) p = 1"
    using count_eq_zero_iff count_filter_mset by (metis (no_types, lifting)) 
  then have pin: "∀ P ∈# {# mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2} | b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b2#}. 
      count P p = 1"
    using count_eq_zero_iff count_filter_mset by blast
  have "?M = {# mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2} | b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b2#} + 
              {# mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2} | b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . ¬ (p ⊆ b2)#}" 
    by (metis image_mset_union multiset_partition) 
  then have "count (∑⇩#?M) p = 
      size {# mset_set {y .y ⊆ blv ∩ b2 ∧ card y = 2} | b2 ∈# (ℬ - {#blv#}) . p ⊆ b2#}" 
    using pin by (auto simp add: count_sum_mset)
  then show ?thesis using size_inter by linarith  
qed

Theorem (Cardinality of Subsets in a Finite Set):
For any finite set \(X\), the number of 2-element subsets (combinations) of \(X\) is equal to the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{2}\), where \(n\) is the cardinality of \(X\).

lemma card_sameprod: "finite X ⟹ card (X^𝟮) = card X choose 2" 
  unfolding sameprod_altdef
  by (subst n_subsets, auto)

Theorem (Cardinality of Universe of Real Numbers):
The set of real numbers, denoted as the continuum (mathbb), has the same cardinality as the set of natural numbers (nat) combined with the set of natural numbers again, which is represented as (nat set set). This implies a bijection exists between the continuum and the set of natural numbers squared, showing that the size of the continuum is equivalent to the sum of the cardinality of natural numbers taken to the power of two.

theorem eqpoll_UNIV_real: "(UNIV :: real set) ≈ (UNIV :: nat set set)"
proof (rule lepoll_antisym)
  show "(UNIV :: nat set set) ≲ (UNIV :: real set)"
    unfolding lepoll_def using inj_nat_set_to_ternary by blast
next
  have "(UNIV :: real set) ≲ (UNIV :: rat set set)"
    unfolding lepoll_def using inj_Dedekind_cut by blast
  also have "… = Pow (UNIV :: rat set)"
    by simp
  also have "… ≈ Pow (UNIV :: nat set)"
    by (rule eqpoll_Pow) (auto simp: infinite_UNIV_char_0 eqpoll_UNIV_nat_iff)
  also have "… = (UNIV :: nat set set)"
    by simp
  finally show "(UNIV :: real set) ≲ (UNIV :: nat set set)" .
qed

Theorem (Cardinality of Multiset Powerset):
Given a finite set A, the cardinality of the multiset powerset (the set of all multisets that can be formed from A) is less than or equal to one plus the cardinality of A.

lemma count_mset_set_leq':
  assumes "finite A"
  shows "count (mset_set A) x ≤ Suc 0"
using assms count_mset_set_leq by fastforce

Theorem (Cardinality of Powers of a Set):
Given a set \(A\), the cardinality of the power set \(Pow A\) (the set of all subsets of \(A\)) is strictly greater than the cardinality of \(A\) itself, as shown by Cantor's theorem.

lemma card_of_Pow: "|A| <o |Pow A|"
  using card_of_ordLess2[of "Pow A" A]  Cantors_theorem[of A]
    Pow_not_empty[of A] by auto

Theorem (Inclusion of Natural Numbers in Finite Sets):
For any natural number \(j\), if \(j\) is an element of the set of all natural numbers up to \(n\) (denoted as \(n \leq i\)), then the number of elements in the set of natural numbers up to \(n\) excluding \(j\) is equal to \(n\).

lemma Nset2finite_inj_tr0:"j ∈ {i. i ≤ (n::nat)} ⟹
                                     card ({i. i ≤ n} - {j}) = n"
by simp

Theorem (Cardinality of a Finite Set):
The cardinality of a finite set is equal to two raised to the power of its cardinality, expressed as \(|A| = 2^{|A|}\), where \(A\) is a finite set.

lemma card_set [simp]: "CARD('a set) = 2 ^ CARD('a::finite)"
by(simp add: card_UNIV_set)

Theorem (Nash-Williams Partition Theorem):
For any infinite set and a collection of finite subsets, if each finite subset is contained within an initial segment of the infinite set, then the infinite set can be partitioned into a finite number of disjoint sets, each corresponding to the finite subsets.

lemma less_sets_UN2: "less_sets A (⋃ ℬ) ⟷ (∀B∈ℬ. A ≪ B)"
  by (auto simp: less_sets_def)
